subject: Mathematics
title: The Cricket Team Selection Mystery
hook: Arjun and Priya organize a school cricket tournament — but who counts as a team member?

slides.title: The Tournament Begins
slides.storyContext: Arjun is selecting his cricket team for the school tournament. He says, 'Our team has Raj, Karan, Priya, and Deepak.' Coach Ramesh asks: 'Arjun, what exactly do you mean by *your* team? Is it fixed? Can you list every member clearly?' Arjun realizes he needs a precise way to describe his group.

image.alt: The Tournament Begins — Sets

slides.title: What is a Set?
slides.storyContext: Coach Ramesh explains: 'A set is just a well-defined collection of distinct objects. In our cricket context, your team is a set.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects called elements.

points.label: Well-defined
points.text: For any object, we can clearly say whether it belongs or doesn't belong.

points.label: Distinct
points.text: No element repeats in a set — we list each only once.

points.label: Notation
points.text: We use capital letters: A, B, C. Elements go in braces: A = {1, 2, 3}.

example.problem: Is 'tall players' a valid set?
example.solution: No — 'tall' is vague. We can't agree on who is tall. A valid set might be {players with height > 180 cm} if we can measure.

slides.inSimpleWords: A set is a clearly defined group where each member either is or is not in it — no maybe.

image.alt: What is a Set? — Sets

slides.title: Representing Sets: Two Methods
slides.storyContext: Priya records the team two ways. Arjun says the names out loud (she writes them), and Coach writes rules on the board.

points.label: Roster Form
points.text: List all elements: A = {Raj, Karan, Priya, Deepak}.

points.label: Set-builder Form
points.text: Write a rule: A = {x | x is a member of our team}.

points.label: Set-builder shorthand
points.text: A = {x | x ∈ cricket team of Class 11A}.

example.problem: Write the set of even single-digit natural numbers both ways.
example.solution: Roster: {2, 4, 6, 8}. Set-builder: {x | x is even and 1 < x < 10}.

slides.inSimpleWords: You can write a set by listing items or by giving a rule that picks them.

slides.title: Empty Set and Special Sets
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'What if no one shows up to a training session?' Coach says, 'That's the empty set — nothing in it.'

points.label: Empty set
points.text: The set with no elements: ∅ or { }.

points.label: Singleton set
points.text: A set with one element: {5}.

points.label: Finite set
points.text: A set with finitely many elements: {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}.

points.label: Infinite set
points.text: A set with infinitely many elements: ℕ = {1, 2, 3, 4, ...}.

example.problem: Is {x | x is a natural number and x < 1} empty?
example.solution: Yes — no natural number is less than 1, so this is ∅.

slides.inSimpleWords: Some sets are empty, some have one item, some have many, some go on forever.

slides.title: Subsets and Equality
slides.storyContext: Arjun's team plays in three formats: Test cricket (5 players), ODI (8 players), T20 (11 players). Arjun notices: 'All Test players also play T20, but not all T20 players play Test.'

points.label: Subset
points.text: A ⊆ B means: every element of A is also in B.

points.label: Proper subset
points.text: A ⊂ B means A ⊆ B but A ≠ B (A is strictly smaller).

points.label: Equal sets
points.text: A = B if A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A (they have the same elements).

example.solution: Yes, because every element of A (1 and 2) is in B. And A ⊂ B (proper subset) because A ≠ B.

slides.inSimpleWords: Subset means all members of one group are also in a bigger group.

slides.title: Union and Intersection
slides.storyContext: Two teams: Team A = {Raj, Karan, Priya} and Team B = {Karan, Deepak, Meera}. Priya asks: 'If both teams play together, who plays? Who is common to both?'

points.label: Union
points.text: A ∪ B = {x | x ∈ A or x ∈ B} — all members of either or both.

points.label: Intersection
points.text: A ∩ B = {x | x ∈ A and x ∈ B} — members in both.

points.label: Disjoint sets
points.text: If A ∩ B = ∅, the sets share no elements.

example.solution: A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4} (all elements from both). A ∩ B = {2, 3} (common elements).

slides.inSimpleWords: Union combines everything from both; intersection picks only what's in both.

slides.title: Full Problem: Venn Diagram Application
slides.storyContext: In a school of 100 students, 60 play cricket, 40 play football, and 15 play both. How many play only cricket? How many play only football? How many play neither?

example.problem: Find the number in each region of a two-set Venn diagram.
example.solution: Let C = cricket players, F = football players. |C| = 60, |F| = 40, |C ∩ F| = 15. Only cricket: 60 − 15 = 45. Only football: 40 − 15 = 25. Both: 15. Neither: 100 − (45 + 25 + 15) = 15 students.

slides.inSimpleWords: Venn diagrams show overlaps clearly — count each region separately.

slides.title: Complement and De Morgan's Laws
slides.storyContext: In Class 11A (total 50 students), the cricket team has 12 members. Coach asks: 'How many students are NOT on the cricket team?'

points.label: Complement
points.text: A' or A^c = {x | x ∉ A} — all elements NOT in A (within a universal set U).

example.solution: A' = {1, 3, 5} (all elements in U not in A).

slides.inSimpleWords: Complement is everything outside a set; De Morgan's laws flip unions and intersections when taking complements.

image.alt: Complement and De Morgan's Laws — Sets

slides.title: Challenge: Team Selection Logic
slides.storyContext: Arjun records: A = {players trained in batting}, B = {players trained in bowling}. Find the roster form if U = {Raj, Karan, Priya, Deepak, Meera, Vikram}, A = {Raj, Karan, Priya}, B = {Karan, Deepak, Meera}.

example.solution: (1) A ∪ B = {Raj, Karan, Priya, Deepak, Meera}. (2) A ∩ B = {Karan}. (3) A' = {Deepak, Meera, Vikram}. (4) (A ∪ B)' = {Vikram}.

slides.inSimpleWords: Apply the operations step by step — first union, then intersection, then complement.

slides.title: Sets: Key Takeaways

points.text: A set is a well-defined, distinct collection of objects.
Represent sets in roster form {a, b, c} or set-builder form {x | condition}.
A ⊆ B means every element of A is in B (subset).
A ∪ B is union (all elements), A ∩ B is intersection (common elements).
A' is the complement (everything outside A in the universal set U).
De Morgan's laws: (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B' and (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B'.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sets organize objects clearly; unions combine, intersections overlap, complements exclude.

subject: Mathematics
title: Pairing Students with Subjects: Relations and Functions
hook: When does a pairing rule become a true function? Arjun and Priya explore the rules.

slides.title: Subject Assignment at School
slides.storyContext: At Class 11A, Priya is assigned students to elective subjects. She tracks: 'Arjun takes Math, Karan takes Physics, Priya takes Math, Deepak takes Chemistry.' Mrs. Sharma asks: 'Is every student taking exactly one subject? Can one student take two subjects?' Priya realizes she needs to formalize this relationship.

image.alt: Subject Assignment at School — Relations and Functions

slides.title: Cartesian Product and Ordered Pairs
slides.storyContext: Priya writes all possible (student, subject) pairs on the board: (Arjun, Math), (Arjun, Physics), (Karan, Math), ...

points.label: Ordered pair
points.text: (a, b) is different from (b, a) — order matters.

points.label: Cartesian product
points.text: A × B = {(a, b) | a ∈ A and b ∈ B} — all possible ordered pairs from A and B.

example.problem: If A = {Ram, Priya} and B = {Math, Physics}, list A × B.
example.solution: A × B = {(Ram, Math), (Ram, Physics), (Priya, Math), (Priya, Physics)}.

slides.inSimpleWords: A Cartesian product pairs every element from the first set with every element from the second.

image.alt: Cartesian Product and Ordered Pairs — Relations and Functions

slides.title: What is a Relation?
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma says: 'A relation is simply a subset of the Cartesian product — some (but not all) pairs from A × B satisfy a rule.'

points.label: Relation definition
points.text: R ⊆ A × B is a relation from A to B.

points.label: Domain
points.text: The set of all first elements in R — the 'input' set.

points.label: Codomain
points.text: The set B (the intended 'output' set).

points.label: Range
points.text: The set of all second elements actually appearing in R — subset of codomain.

example.problem: Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and R = {(1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6), (4, 8)} (the 'double' relation). Find domain, codomain, range.
example.solution: Domain = {1, 2, 3, 4}. Codomain = ℕ (all natural numbers, assumed). Range = {2, 4, 6, 8}.

slides.inSimpleWords: A relation picks some pairs from a Cartesian product according to a rule.

slides.title: What is a Function?
slides.storyContext: Priya says: 'Wait — can one student take two subjects at the same time?' Mrs. Sharma: 'If we're assigning ELECTIVES, each student takes exactly one. That's a function.'

points.label: Function definition
points.text: f: A → B is a relation where EVERY element of A maps to EXACTLY ONE element of B.

points.label: Notation
points.text: f(x) = y means the element x maps to y.

points.label: Test
points.text: A relation R is a function if no element of domain appears twice in the pairs.

example.solution: No — 1 maps to both 2 and 4. Each input must have exactly one output.

slides.inSimpleWords: A function gives each input exactly one output — no input can have two answers.

slides.title: Types of Functions: Injective, Surjective, Bijective
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: 'Can two students take the same subject? Can a subject have no student?' Mrs. Sharma introduces three types.

points.label: Injective (one-to-one)
points.text: If f(a) = f(b), then a = b. Different inputs → different outputs.

points.label: Surjective (onto)
points.text: Every element of B is the image of some element in A (range = codomain).

points.label: Bijective
points.text: Both injective and surjective — a perfect one-to-one matching.

example.problem: f: {1, 2, 3} → {a, b, c} with f(1)=a, f(2)=b, f(3)=c. Is f bijective?
example.solution: Yes — f is injective (each input maps to a different output) and surjective (every element in codomain is hit). So f is bijective.

slides.inSimpleWords: Injective = no sharing outputs; surjective = all outputs are used; bijective = both.

slides.title: Composition of Functions
slides.storyContext: Arjun takes subject Math (function f), which has a difficulty level: Math → Level 3 (function g). Priya asks: 'What if I combine the two assignments?'

points.label: Composition
points.text: (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)) — apply f first, then g to the result.

points.label: Condition
points.text: f: A → B and g: B → C, then g ∘ f: A → C.

points.label: Order matters
points.text: f ∘ g is usually different from g ∘ f (not commutative).

example.problem: f(x) = 2x and g(x) = x + 3. Find (g ∘ f)(5) and (f ∘ g)(5).

slides.inSimpleWords: Composition chains functions — output of the first becomes input of the second.

slides.title: Inverse Functions
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma: 'If Arjun's Math assignment is f, can we reverse it? If we know his subject is Math, can we get Arjun back?'

points.label: Inverse function
points.text: f⁻¹: B → A exists only if f is bijective.

points.label: Property
points.text: f⁻¹(f(x)) = x and f(f⁻¹(y)) = y.

points.label: Finding inverse
points.text: Set y = f(x), solve for x in terms of y, swap variables.

example.problem: If f(x) = 2x + 3, find f⁻¹.
example.solution: Set y = 2x + 3. Solve: x = (y − 3)/2. Swap: f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2.

slides.inSimpleWords: An inverse function 'undoes' the original — if f sends x to y, f⁻¹ sends y back to x.

slides.title: Full Problem: Verifying Bijection and Finding Inverse
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma defines f: {1, 2, 3} → {5, 7, 9} by f(x) = 2x + 3. She asks: 'Is f bijective? Find f⁻¹.'

example.problem: Check if f is injective and surjective, then find f⁻¹.
example.solution: f(1) = 5, f(2) = 7, f(3) = 9. All different (injective). All elements {5, 7, 9} are hit (surjective). So f is bijective. f⁻¹(5) = 1, f⁻¹(7) = 2, f⁻¹(9) = 3, or f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2.

slides.inSimpleWords: To verify bijection, check that every input has one output and every output comes from one input.

slides.title: Challenge: Composition and Injectivity
slides.storyContext: Given f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = 2x, find (f ∘ g) and (g ∘ f). Verify that both are injective.

example.problem: Compute (f ∘ g)(x) and (g ∘ f)(x). Are both injective?
example.solution: (f ∘ g)(x) = f(2x) = 2x + 1. (g ∘ f)(x) = g(x + 1) = 2(x + 1) = 2x + 2. Both are injective because if 2x₁ + 1 = 2x₂ + 1, then x₁ = x₂.

slides.inSimpleWords: Check injectivity by assuming f(a) = f(b) and proving a = b.

slides.title: Relations and Functions: Key Takeaways

points.text: A Cartesian product A × B is all ordered pairs (a, b) with a ∈ A, b ∈ B.
A relation is any subset of a Cartesian product.
A function f: A → B is a relation where every element of A maps to exactly one element of B.
Domain = inputs; codomain = intended outputs; range = actual outputs.
Injective = different inputs → different outputs. Surjective = all codomain elements are hit.
Bijective functions have inverses; composition chains functions (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)).

slides.inSimpleWords: Functions map each input to exactly one output; special types (injective, surjective, bijective) impose stronger conditions.

image.alt: Relations and Functions: Key Takeaways — Relations and Functions

subject: Mathematics
title: Angles and Shadows: Trigonometry in Daily Life
hook: From measuring temple heights to tracking the sun's angle — trigonometric functions are everywhere.

image.alt: Trigonometric Functions: Angles and Ratios — Trigonometric Functions

slides.title: Measuring the School Temple Height
slides.storyContext: Arjun stands 20 meters from a temple and measures the angle of elevation to the top as 45°. Priya says: 'We can find the height without climbing!' Mr. Kapoor, a surveyor, explains: 'This is trigonometry — the mathematics of angles and sides.'

slides.title: Angle Measurement: Degrees and Radians
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor teaches: 'Angles can be measured two ways — degrees (what you see on a protractor) and radians (mathematical standard).'

points.label: Degree
points.text: 1° = 1/360 of a full rotation. A straight angle = 180°.

points.label: Radian
points.text: 1 radian = angle at center of circle when arc length = radius. π radians = 180°.

points.label: Conversion
points.text: Degrees = (radians) × (180/π). Radians = (degrees) × (π/180).

example.problem: Convert 90° and π/3 radians to the other unit.

slides.inSimpleWords: Degrees divide a circle into 360 parts; radians use the radius length as the natural unit.

slides.title: Sine, Cosine, and Tangent: The Big Three
slides.storyContext: Arjun draws a right triangle. Mr. Kapoor labels: opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse. 'These ratios between sides are the trig functions.'

points.label: sine θ
points.text: sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse.

points.label: cosine θ
points.text: cos θ = adjacent / hypotenuse.

points.label: tangent θ
points.text: tan θ = opposite / adjacent = sin θ / cos θ.

points.label: Reciprocals
points.text: csc θ = 1/sin θ, sec θ = 1/cos θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ.

example.problem: In a right triangle with opposite = 3, adjacent = 4, hypotenuse = 5. Find sin θ, cos θ, tan θ.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sine, cosine, and tangent are just ratios of triangle sides — memorize which side goes on top.

image.alt: Sine, Cosine, and Tangent: The Big Three — Trigonometric Functions

slides.title: Unit Circle and Trig Functions for Any Angle
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'But what if the angle is 120° or 270°? There's no right triangle.' Mr. Kapoor draws a unit circle (radius 1). 'The angle's sine and cosine are simply the y and x coordinates of the point on the circle.'

points.label: Unit circle
points.text: Circle of radius 1 centered at origin. Point on circle: (cos θ, sin θ).

points.label: For any angle
points.text: cos θ = x-coordinate, sin θ = y-coordinate of point at angle θ.

points.label: Ranges
points.text: −1 ≤ sin θ ≤ 1 and −1 ≤ cos θ ≤ 1 for all θ.

points.label: Identity
points.text: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 (Pythagorean identity).

example.problem: On the unit circle, find sin 90°, cos 90°, sin 180°, cos 180°.

slides.inSimpleWords: The unit circle extends trig functions to all angles by using coordinates of points on the circle.

slides.title: Trigonometric Values of Special Angles
slides.storyContext: Arjun memorizes: '0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90° are special. Their trig values come up in exams constantly.'

points.label: Memorization
points.text: Use the hand trick or a table — these values repeat in all quadrants (with sign changes).

example.solution: sin 135° = sin(180° − 45°) = sin 45° = 1/√2 (sine is positive in quadrants 1 and 2).

slides.inSimpleWords: Memorize the special angles 30°, 45°, 60° — they appear constantly in problems.

image.alt: Trigonometric Values of Special Angles — Trigonometric Functions

slides.title: Periodicity and Graphs of Trig Functions
slides.storyContext: Priya plots sin θ on a graph. 'It goes up and down, repeating every 360°!' Mr. Kapoor: 'That's periodicity — sin(θ + 360°) = sin θ.'

points.label: Period of sine
points.text: sin(θ + 2π) = sin θ (period = 360° or 2π radians).

points.label: Period of cosine
points.text: cos(θ + 2π) = cos θ (period = 360° or 2π radians).

points.label: Period of tangent
points.text: tan(θ + π) = tan θ (period = 180° or π radians).

points.label: Amplitude
points.text: Max and min of sine/cosine are ±1 (amplitude = 1).

slides.inSimpleWords: Trig functions repeat periodically — adding 360° (or 2π) to sine/cosine gives the same value.

image.alt: Periodicity and Graphs of Trig Functions — Trigonometric Functions

slides.title: Full Problem: Height of the Temple
slides.storyContext: Arjun stands 20 m from the temple base. The angle of elevation to the top is 45°. Find the height.

example.problem: In a right triangle: angle at ground = 45°, adjacent side = 20 m. Find the opposite side (height).
example.solution: tan 45° = opposite / adjacent. 1 = height / 20. height = 20 meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: Set up the right triangle, identify the known angle and side, use the correct trig ratio, solve.

slides.title: Angles of Elevation and Depression
slides.storyContext: Arjun is on a bridge 30 m high, looking down at Priya on the ground 40 m away. The angle of depression is what Arjun sees; the angle of elevation is what Priya sees looking up.

points.label: Angle of elevation
points.text: Angle above the horizontal when looking UP at an object.

points.label: Angle of depression
points.text: Angle below the horizontal when looking DOWN at an object.

points.label: Key insight
points.text: Angle of elevation from A = Angle of depression from B (alternate interior angles).

example.problem: From a 30 m bridge, the angle of depression to a boat is 60°. How far is the boat from the bridge base?
example.solution: tan 60° = 30 / distance. √3 = 30 / distance. distance = 30/√3 = 10√3 meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: Elevation is looking up; depression is looking down. They're related by geometry.

image.alt: Angles of Elevation and Depression — Trigonometric Functions

slides.title: Challenge: Two-angle Problem
slides.storyContext: From a point on the ground 100 m from a building, the angle of elevation to the top is 30°. If Arjun moves 50 m closer, the angle becomes 45°. Find the building height using both angles.

example.problem: From 100 m: tan 30° = h/100. From 50 m: tan 45° = h/50. Verify consistency and solve.
example.solution: From first: h = 100 tan 30° = 100/√3 ≈ 57.7 m. From second: h = 50 tan 45° = 50 m. These don't match — the problem setup is inconsistent. (In real problems, both angles give the same h.)

slides.inSimpleWords: Set up trig equations from each observation angle, solve simultaneously if needed.

image.alt: Challenge: Two-angle Problem — Trigonometric Functions

slides.title: Trigonometric Functions: Key Takeaways

points.text: sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan θ = opposite/adjacent.
Convert between degrees and radians: 180° = π radians.
Unit circle: (cos θ, sin θ) are coordinates at angle θ; sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.
Special angles: 30°, 45°, 60° have exact trig values — memorize them.
Trig functions are periodic: sin/cos repeat every 360° (2π); tan repeats every 180° (π).
Angle of elevation = looking up; angle of depression = looking down.

slides.inSimpleWords: Trig functions relate angles to side ratios; they repeat periodically and solve real-world height/distance problems.

image.alt: Trigonometric Functions: Key Takeaways — Trigonometric Functions

subject: Mathematics
title: Imaginary Treasures: Complex Numbers Unlock Solutions
hook: Not all quadratic equations have real solutions — complex numbers complete the picture.

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: Student puzzled by negative square roots

image.alt: Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations — Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations

slides.title: The Unsolvable Quadratic
slides.storyContext: Arjun tries to solve x² + 1 = 0, which gives x² = −1. He says: 'Square roots of negative numbers don't exist!' Dr. Patel smiles: 'What if we invent a new number i where i² = −1? That's the gateway to complex numbers.'

image.alt: The Unsolvable Quadratic — Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations

slides.title: The Imaginary Unit and Complex Numbers
slides.storyContext: Dr. Patel defines: 'The imaginary unit i satisfies i² = −1. Any number a + bi (a, b real) is a complex number.'

points.label: Complex number
points.text: z = a + bi where a, b ∈ ℝ. a is the real part, b is the imaginary part.

points.label: Real numbers
points.text: Special case: if b = 0, then z = a (purely real).

points.label: Purely imaginary
points.text: If a = 0, then z = bi (purely imaginary).

example.problem: Identify the real and imaginary parts of 3 + 4i.
example.solution: Real part = 3, imaginary part = 4.

slides.inSimpleWords: A complex number is just 'real part + imaginary part,' where the imaginary part uses i.

slides.title: Algebra with Complex Numbers: Addition and Multiplication
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'Can we add, subtract, multiply complex numbers like we do with real numbers?' Dr. Patel: 'Yes, just keep i² = −1 in mind when multiplying.'

points.label: Addition
points.text: (a + bi) + (c + di) = (a + c) + (b + d)i.

points.label: Subtraction
points.text: (a + bi) − (c + di) = (a − c) + (b − d)i.

points.label: Multiplication
points.text: (a + bi)(c + di) = ac + adi + bci + bdi² = (ac − bd) + (ad + bc)i (remember i² = −1).

example.problem: Compute (2 + 3i)(1 − 2i).

slides.inSimpleWords: Add real parts to real parts, imaginary to imaginary. When multiplying, use i² = −1 to simplify.

image.alt: Algebra with Complex Numbers: Addition and Multiplication — Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations

slides.title: Complex Conjugate and Division
slides.storyContext: To divide complex numbers, Dr. Patel multiplies by the conjugate: if z = a + bi, the conjugate z̄ = a − bi.

points.label: Conjugate
points.text: If z = a + bi, then z̄ = a − bi.

points.label: Property
points.text: z · z̄ = a² + b² (always real and positive).

points.label: Division
points.text: To divide z₁/z₂, multiply by z̄₂/z̄₂: (z₁/z₂) = (z₁ · z̄₂)/(z₂ · z̄₂).

example.problem: Compute (2 + i)/(1 + i).

slides.inSimpleWords: To divide, multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator.

image.alt: Complex Conjugate and Division — Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations

slides.title: Modulus and Argument
slides.storyContext: Priya visualizes complex numbers on a plane (real axis horizontal, imaginary axis vertical). 'The distance from origin is the modulus; the angle is the argument.'

points.label: Modulus
points.text: |z| = |a + bi| = √(a² + b²).

points.label: Argument
points.text: arg(z) = angle θ from positive real axis. z = |z|(cos θ + i sin θ).

points.label: Polar form
points.text: z = r(cos θ + i sin θ) or z = r e^(iθ), where r = |z|, θ = arg(z).

example.problem: Find the modulus and argument of 3 + 4i.

slides.inSimpleWords: Modulus is the distance from origin; argument is the angle from the positive real axis.

image.alt: Modulus and Argument — Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations

slides.title: Solving Quadratic Equations with Complex Roots
slides.storyContext: Arjun solves x² + 2x + 5 = 0. The discriminant Δ = 4 − 20 = −16 < 0. Dr. Patel: 'No real solutions, but complex solutions exist.'

points.label: Discriminant Δ
points.text: Δ = b² − 4ac. If Δ < 0, roots are complex conjugates.

points.label: Complex roots
points.text: If Δ < 0, roots = [−b ± i√|Δ|] / (2a).

example.problem: Solve x² + 2x + 5 = 0.

slides.inSimpleWords: When the discriminant is negative, the quadratic has complex conjugate roots.

image.alt: Solving Quadratic Equations with Complex Roots — Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations

slides.title: Full Problem: Quadratic with Complex Roots
slides.storyContext: Solve 2x² − 4x + 3 = 0 and verify your solutions.

example.problem: Use the quadratic formula to find all roots.

slides.inSimpleWords: Substitute into the quadratic formula; simplify radicals; express in the form a + bi.

image.alt: Full Problem: Quadratic with Complex Roots — Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations

slides.title: De Moivre's Theorem and Powers of Complex Numbers
slides.storyContext: Priya raises 1 + i to the 10th power. In rectangular form, it's tedious. But using polar form and De Moivre's theorem: (r e^(iθ))^n = r^n e^(i n θ).

points.label: De Moivre's theorem
points.text: [r(cos θ + i sin θ)]^n = r^n(cos nθ + i sin nθ).

points.label: Application
points.text: Raise complex numbers to powers efficiently using polar form.

points.label: nth roots
points.text: For z = r e^(iθ), the nth roots are r^(1/n) e^(i(θ + 2πk)/n), k = 0, 1, ..., n−1.

example.problem: Find (1 + i)⁴.

slides.inSimpleWords: Convert to polar form, apply De Moivre's theorem, convert back to rectangular form.

image.alt: De Moivre's Theorem and Powers of Complex Numbers — Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations

slides.title: Challenge: Solving a Cubic with One Real Root
slides.storyContext: Solve x³ − 1 = 0. One root is x = 1; the other two are complex.

example.problem: Factor x³ − 1 = (x − 1)(x² + x + 1) and find all three roots.
example.solution: From x − 1 = 0: x = 1. From x² + x + 1 = 0: Δ = 1 − 4 = −3. x = [−1 ± i√3] / 2 (the complex cube roots of unity).

slides.inSimpleWords: Factor the cubic, then solve each factor — some factors yield complex roots.

image.alt: Challenge: Solving a Cubic with One Real Root — Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations

slides.title: Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations: Key Takeaways

points.text: i² = −1; a complex number z = a + bi has real part a and imaginary part b.
Add complex numbers term by term; multiply using i² = −1.
To divide, multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator.
Modulus |a + bi| = √(a² + b²); argument is the angle θ from the positive real axis.
If the discriminant of a quadratic is negative, the roots are complex conjugates.
De Moivre's theorem: [r(cos θ + i sin θ)]^n = r^n(cos nθ + i sin nθ).

slides.inSimpleWords: Complex numbers extend the real numbers to solve all quadratics; they combine with algebra, trigonometry, and power laws.

image.alt: Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations: Key Takeaways — Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations

subject: Mathematics
chapterAliases: Linear Inequalities in One and Two Variables
title: Dividing the Market: Linear Inequalities in Budgets and Boundaries
hook: When resources are limited, inequalities define what's possible — not just exact answers.

image.alt: Linear Inequalities: Solutions and Regions — Linear Inequalities

slides.title: Budgeting for the Festival Stall
slides.storyContext: Arjun runs a fruit stall at the village fair. He has ₹500 to spend on apples (₹40 each) and oranges (₹30 each). Priya asks: 'How many of each can we buy?' Mr. Gupta explains: 'That's not one answer — it's a range of possibilities governed by an inequality.'

image.alt: Budgeting for the Festival Stall — Linear Inequalities

slides.title: Inequalities: Meaning and Notation
slides.storyContext: Mr. Gupta writes on the board: x > 5, y ≤ 10, z ≠ 3. 'Each symbol defines a relationship between quantities.'

points.label: Greater than
points.text: a > b means a is strictly larger than b.

points.label: Greater than or equal
points.text: a ≥ b means a is larger than or equal to b.

points.label: Less than
points.text: a < b means a is strictly smaller than b.

points.label: Less than or equal
points.text: a ≤ b means a is smaller than or equal to b.

example.problem: Is x = 5 a solution to x > 3 and x ≤ 10?
example.solution: Yes to both: 5 > 3 (true) and 5 ≤ 10 (true).

slides.inSimpleWords: An inequality is a statement about relative size, solved by finding all values that make it true.

image.alt: Inequalities: Meaning and Notation — Linear Inequalities

slides.title: Solving Linear Inequalities in One Variable
slides.storyContext: Arjun wants apples to cost less than ₹300: 40x < 300. Priya solves: x < 7.5, so he can buy at most 7 apples.

points.label: Addition/Subtraction
points.text: Add or subtract the same number from both sides; inequality sign stays the same.

points.label: Multiplication/Division
points.text: Multiply or divide by positive numbers: sign stays the same. By negative numbers: FLIP the sign.

points.label: Solution set
points.text: Write as x > 5 or in interval notation: (5, ∞).

example.problem: Solve −2x + 5 > 9.
example.solution: −2x > 4. Divide by −2 (flip sign): x < −2. Solution: x ∈ (−∞, −2).

slides.inSimpleWords: Solve inequalities like equations, but flip the sign when multiplying/dividing by negatives.

image.alt: Solving Linear Inequalities in One Variable — Linear Inequalities

slides.title: Compound Inequalities and Interval Notation
slides.storyContext: Arjun says: 'I want to buy between 5 and 10 apples.' This is 5 ≤ x ≤ 10. Mr. Gupta: 'That's a compound inequality — two conditions at once.'

points.label: AND (conjunction)
points.text: Both conditions must be true. 2 < x < 5 means x > 2 AND x < 5.

points.label: OR (disjunction)
points.text: At least one condition is true. x < 0 OR x > 10.

points.label: Interval notation
points.text: (a, b) = a < x < b (open). [a, b] = a ≤ x ≤ b (closed). [a, b) = a ≤ x < b (half-open).

example.problem: Write in interval notation: 3 < x ≤ 7.

slides.inSimpleWords: Compound inequalities combine two ranges; intervals use parentheses (open) and brackets (closed).

slides.title: Linear Inequalities in Two Variables
slides.storyContext: Arjun's budget: 40x + 30y ≤ 500 (where x = apples, y = oranges). Priya plots this on a graph. 'The solution is a whole region, not just a line.'

points.label: Equation of boundary
points.text: 40x + 30y = 500 is the boundary line.

points.label: Solution region
points.text: All points (x, y) where 40x + 30y ≤ 500 (including the line).

points.label: Test point
points.text: Pick (0, 0). If 0 ≤ 500 (true), shade the region containing (0, 0).

points.label: Boundary type
points.text: Use solid line for ≤ or ≥; dashed line for < or >.

example.problem: Graph 2x + y > 4.
example.solution: Line: 2x + y = 4 (dashed). Test (0, 0): 0 > 4 (false), so shade the region NOT containing (0, 0).

slides.inSimpleWords: Plot the boundary line; test a point to decide which side to shade; use solid or dashed based on ≤/< or >/≥.

image.alt: Linear Inequalities in Two Variables — Linear Inequalities

slides.title: Full Problem: Two-Variable Budget Optimization
slides.storyContext: Arjun has ₹500. Apples cost ₹40, oranges cost ₹30. He wants at least 5 apples and at least 3 oranges. Graph the feasible region and find one valid purchase.

example.problem: Graph and find a point in the region: 40x + 30y ≤ 500, x ≥ 5, y ≥ 3.
example.solution: Boundary lines: 40x + 30y = 500 (passing through (12.5, 0) and (0, 16.67)), x = 5 (vertical), y = 3 (horizontal). Feasible region is bounded by these three lines. One valid point: (5, 8) gives cost = 40(5) + 30(8) = 200 + 240 = ₹440 ≤ ₹500.

slides.inSimpleWords: Set up all constraints as inequalities, plot the boundary lines, shade the feasible region, pick a point inside.

slides.title: Systems of Linear Inequalities in Two Variables
slides.storyContext: Mr. Gupta adds constraints: x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 (can't buy negative quantities). Priya visualizes: 'The solution is the intersection of all constraint regions.'

points.label: System
points.text: Multiple inequalities solved simultaneously.

points.label: Solution region
points.text: The intersection (overlap) of all individual solution regions.

points.label: Vertices
points.text: Key points are where boundary lines intersect — often optimal points.

example.problem: Solve: x + y ≤ 5, x ≥ 1, y ≥ 0.
example.solution: Graph all three boundaries. Feasible region is bounded by x = 1 (left), y = 0 (bottom), and x + y = 5 (upper boundary). Vertices: (1, 0), (1, 4), (5, 0).

slides.inSimpleWords: Graph all inequalities; the solution is where all shaded regions overlap.

slides.title: Linear Programming: Maximizing Profit
slides.storyContext: Arjun profits ₹10 per apple and ₹8 per orange. He wants to maximize profit subject to his budget and minimum quantities. This is linear programming.

points.label: Objective function
points.text: Maximize or minimize: P = 10x + 8y (profit).

points.label: Constraints
points.text: Subject to: 40x + 30y ≤ 500, x ≥ 5, y ≥ 3, x, y ≥ 0.

points.label: Optimal solution
points.text: Usually found at a vertex of the feasible region.

example.problem: Maximize P = 10x + 8y subject to 40x + 30y ≤ 500, x ≥ 5, y ≥ 3.
example.solution: Check vertices of feasible region. E.g., at (5, 10): P = 50 + 80 = 130. At (12.5, 0): P = 125. The maximum is at one of the vertices — test all.

slides.inSimpleWords: Find the vertex of the feasible region that gives the maximum (or minimum) value of the objective function.

slides.title: Challenge: Business Decision Making
slides.storyContext: Arjun wants to maximize profit P = 10x + 8y subject to 40x + 30y ≤ 500, x ≥ 5, y ≥ 3. Find the optimal purchase.

example.problem: List all vertices of the feasible region and evaluate the objective at each.

slides.inSimpleWords: Evaluate the objective function at every vertex of the feasible region; the best vertex is the optimal solution.

slides.title: Linear Inequalities: Key Takeaways

points.text: Solve one-variable inequalities like equations; flip the sign when multiplying/dividing by negatives.
Compound inequalities combine two ranges (AND/OR); write solutions in interval notation.
In two variables, graph the boundary line and shade the region satisfying the inequality.
Use solid lines for ≤, ≥; use dashed lines for <, >.
Systems of inequalities: graph all constraints and find their intersection (feasible region).
Linear programming: maximize/minimize an objective function over a feasible region; optimal point is usually a vertex.

slides.inSimpleWords: Inequalities describe ranges and regions; systems combine multiple constraints; linear programming optimizes an objective.

image.alt: Linear Inequalities: Key Takeaways — Linear Inequalities

subject: Mathematics
title: Arranging Friends and Choosing Teams: Counting Principles
hook: How many ways can you arrange or select? Permutations and combinations count it all.

slides.title: Permutations and Combinations: Counting Arrangements and Selections
Planning the School Talent Show
slides.storyContext: Arjun is organizing the talent show. 'In how many orders can 3 singers perform?' Priya asks: 'Or if we're picking 2 dancers from 5, how many ways?' Prof. Sharma: 'One counts arrangements (order matters), the other counts selections (order doesn't). Both use factorials and formulas.'

slides.title: Factorial Notation
slides.storyContext: Prof. Sharma writes: 5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120. 'Factorial is the foundation of counting.'

points.label: Special cases
points.text: 0! = 1 (by definition). 1! = 1.

points.label: Growth
points.text: n! grows very quickly: 5! = 120, 10! = 3,628,800.

example.problem: Calculate 4! and 6!.

slides.inSimpleWords: Factorial n! is the product of all positive integers from 1 to n.

slides.title: Permutations: Order Matters
slides.storyContext: Arjun has 5 singers but only 3 performance slots. 'How many different orderings are there?' Prof. Sharma: 'That's a permutation: P(5, 3).'

points.label: Permutation definition
points.text: An arrangement of objects where ORDER MATTERS.

points.label: Formula
points.text: P(n, r) = n! / (n−r)! — number of ways to arrange r objects from n.

points.label: Meaning
points.text: P(n, r) counts ordered selections of r items from n items.

points.label: All together
points.text: P(n, n) = n! (arranging all n objects).

example.problem: How many ways can 3 singers perform in order from 5 singers?

slides.inSimpleWords: Permutation P(n, r) counts ordered arrangements; the first position has n choices, second has n−1, etc.

slides.title: Combinations: Order Doesn't Matter
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'I need to pick 2 dancers for a duet from 5 dancers. How many ways can I choose them? The order doesn't matter — (Raj, Karan) is the same team as (Karan, Raj).'

points.label: Combination definition
points.text: A selection of objects where ORDER DOES NOT MATTER.

points.label: Formula
points.text: C(n, r) = n! / [r! × (n−r)!] — number of ways to choose r objects from n.

points.label: Notation
points.text: Also written as ⁿCᵣ or (ⁿ_ᵣ).

points.label: Relationship
points.text: C(n, r) = P(n, r) / r! (divide out the ordering of r items).

example.problem: How many ways can we choose 2 dancers from 5?

slides.inSimpleWords: Combination C(n, r) counts unordered selections; divide permutations by r! to remove the importance of order.

slides.title: Fundamental Counting Principle
slides.storyContext: Arjun designs event programs. 'There are 3 venues, 4 time slots, and 2 themes. How many programs are possible?' Prof. Sharma: 'Multiply: 3 × 4 × 2 = 24.'

points.label: Principle
points.text: If task 1 has m ways and task 2 has n ways, together they have m × n ways.

points.label: Generalization
points.text: For k tasks with n₁, n₂, ..., nₖ ways: total = n₁ × n₂ × ... × nₖ.

points.label: Without replacement
points.text: If one choice affects the next, update the count for each step.

example.problem: A password has 2 digits (0–9), then 3 letters (A–Z). How many passwords?
example.solution: First digit: 10 choices. Second digit: 10 choices. First letter: 26 choices. Second letter: 26 choices. Third letter: 26 choices. Total: 10 × 10 × 26 × 26 × 26 = 17,576,000.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply the number of ways for each step to get the total number of ways for all steps combined.

slides.title: Full Problem: Seating Arrangement at a Dinner
slides.storyContext: A school dinner has 8 teachers and 10 students. Seats are arranged as: 1 head teacher, then 4 teachers on the left, 4 students on the right. How many seating arrangements?

example.problem: Count arrangements: pick 1 head teacher from 8, arrange 4 teachers from remaining 7, arrange 4 students from 10.
example.solution: Head teacher: 8 choices. Remaining 4 teachers from 7: P(7, 4) = 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 = 840. 4 students from 10: P(10, 4) = 10 × 9 × 8 × 7 = 5,040. Total: 8 × 840 × 5,040 = 33,868,800.

slides.inSimpleWords: Break into sub-problems; use permutation for ordered positions; multiply the counts.

slides.title: Permutations with Repetition
slides.storyContext: Arjun assigns 5 students to 3 subjects, allowing each student to take multiple subjects. 'How many assignments?' Prof. Sharma: 'Each student has 3 choices independently, so 3⁵.'

points.label: Formula
points.text: Number of arrangements of n objects chosen from k types (with repetition): kⁿ.

points.label: Interpretation
points.text: Each of n positions has k independent choices.

points.label: Example
points.text: 3-letter codes from alphabet: 26 × 26 × 26 = 26³.

example.problem: How many 4-letter sequences can be formed from {A, B, C}?
example.solution: Each position has 3 choices: 3⁴ = 81.

slides.inSimpleWords: With repetition allowed, each position has the full set of choices; multiply for each position.

slides.title: Permutations with Identical Objects
slides.storyContext: Arjun arranges 5 flags: 2 red, 2 blue, 1 green. 'How many distinct arrangements?' Prof. Sharma: 'Divide by factorials of repetitions: 5! / (2! × 2! × 1!).'

points.label: Formula
points.text: Arrangements of n objects where n₁ are identical, n₂ are identical, ...: n! / (n₁! × n₂! × ...).

points.label: Intuition
points.text: Start with n!, then divide out overcounting due to swaps of identical items.

example.problem: Arrange the letters in BOOK.
example.solution: 4 letters, but O appears twice. Arrangements = 4! / 2! = 24 / 2 = 12.

slides.inSimpleWords: Count total permutations, then divide by factorials of the multiplicities of identical objects.

slides.title: Challenge: Mixed Counting Problem
slides.storyContext: A school committee has 8 people. They must elect a president (1 person), then choose a 3-person subcommittee from the remaining 7. How many ways?

example.problem: Find the number of ways to elect president and then select a subcommittee.
example.solution: President: 8 choices. Subcommittee from remaining 7: C(7, 3) = 7! / (3! × 4!) = 35. Total: 8 × 35 = 280.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use multiplication for sequential tasks; use P or C based on whether order matters within each task.

slides.title: Permutations and Combinations: Key Takeaways

points.text: Permutation P(n, r) = n! / (n−r)! — arrangements where ORDER MATTERS.
Combination C(n, r) = n! / [r! × (n−r)!] — selections where ORDER DOES NOT MATTER.
Fundamental counting principle: multiply the choices for each step.
With repetition: k^n arrangements of n items from k types.
With identical objects: divide by factorials of multiplicities.

slides.inSimpleWords: Permutations count ordered arrangements; combinations count unordered selections; use the counting principle for multi-step problems.

subject: Mathematics
title: Expanding Powers: The Binomial Theorem Explained
hook: How to expand (a + b)ⁿ without endless multiplication? The binomial theorem gives the formula.

slides.title: The Binomial Theorem: Expanding and Patterns
Expanding (x + y)¹⁰ by Hand
slides.storyContext: Arjun tries to expand (x + y)¹⁰ by multiplying out repeatedly. After (x + y)⁴, he's exhausted. Priya says: 'There's a pattern in the coefficients!' Dr. Verma reveals: 'That's Pascal's triangle and the binomial theorem — they give the expansion directly.'

image.alt: Expanding (x + y)¹⁰ by Hand — Binomial Theorem

slides.title: Pascal's Triangle and Binomial Coefficients
slides.storyContext: Dr. Verma draws Pascal's triangle: row 0 is 1; row 1 is 1 1; row 2 is 1 2 1; row 3 is 1 3 3 1. 'Each entry is ⁿCᵣ.'

points.label: Pascal's triangle
points.text: Row n, position r: entry = ⁿCᵣ (binomial coefficient).

points.label: Symmetry
points.text: ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ (triangle is symmetric).

points.label: Row sum
points.text: Sum of row n: ⁿC₀ + ⁿC₁ + ... + ⁿCₙ = 2ⁿ.

example.problem: Find row 4 of Pascal's triangle (coefficients for (a + b)⁴).
example.solution: ⁴C₀ = 1, ⁴C₁ = 4, ⁴C₂ = 6, ⁴C₃ = 4, ⁴C₄ = 1. Row: 1 4 6 4 1.

slides.inSimpleWords: Pascal's triangle contains all binomial coefficients; ⁿCᵣ is the number of ways to choose r from n.

image.alt: Pascal's Triangle and Binomial Coefficients — Binomial Theorem

slides.title: The Binomial Theorem: Statement and Formula
slides.storyContext: Dr. Verma writes the theorem: (a + b)ⁿ = Σ ⁿCᵣ aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ, r = 0 to n.

points.label: Binomial theorem
points.text: (a + b)ⁿ = Σ (from r=0 to n) [ⁿCᵣ × aⁿ⁻ʳ × bʳ].

points.label: General term
points.text: Tᵣ₊₁ = ⁿCᵣ × aⁿ⁻ʳ × bʳ (the (r+1)th term).

points.label: First few terms
points.text: aⁿ + n·aⁿ⁻¹·b + [n(n−1)/2]·aⁿ⁻²·b² + ...

points.label: Special case
points.text: If a = b = 1: (1 + 1)ⁿ = 2ⁿ = sum of all binomial coefficients.

example.problem: Expand (x + 2)³ using the binomial theorem.
example.solution: (x + 2)³ = ³C₀ x³ 2⁰ + ³C₁ x² 2¹ + ³C₂ x¹ 2² + ³C₃ x⁰ 2³ = x³ + 3x² × 2 + 3x × 4 + 8 = x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8.

slides.inSimpleWords: The binomial theorem expands (a + b)ⁿ into a sum of terms using binomial coefficients.

slides.title: Finding Specific Terms
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: 'In the expansion of (a + b)¹⁰, what is the 5th term? Do I have to expand everything?' Priya: 'No — use the general term formula directly.'

points.label: General term
points.text: Tᵣ₊₁ = ⁿCᵣ aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ (the (r+1)th term from the left).

points.label: Middle term
points.text: If n is even: T_{n/2 + 1}. If n is odd: T_{(n+1)/2} and T_{(n+3)/2} (two middle terms).

points.label: Last term
points.text: Tₙ₊₁ = ⁿCₙ aⁿ⁻ⁿ bⁿ = bⁿ.

example.problem: Find the 5th term in (2x + 3y)⁸.
example.solution: 5th term = T₅ = ⁸C₄ (2x)⁸⁻⁴ (3y)⁴ = ⁸C₄ (2x)⁴ (3y)⁴ = 70 × 16x⁴ × 81y⁴ = 90,720 x⁴y⁴.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use Tᵣ₊₁ = ⁿCᵣ aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ to extract individual terms without expanding fully.

image.alt: Finding Specific Terms — Binomial Theorem

slides.title: Binomial Theorem for Rational and Negative Powers
slides.storyContext: Dr. Verma generalizes: 'The binomial theorem works for non-integer n too, but the series is infinite.' She writes: (1 + x)ⁿ = 1 + nx + [n(n−1)/2]x² + ..., valid for |x| < 1.

points.label: Binomial series
points.text: (1 + x)ⁿ = Σ (from r=0 to ∞) [ⁿCᵣ xʳ], valid for |x| < 1.

points.label: Non-integer n
points.text: ⁿCᵣ = [n(n−1)(n−2)...(n−r+1)] / r! (generalized binomial coefficient).

example.problem: Find the first four terms of (1 + x)⁻².

slides.inSimpleWords: The binomial series extends to non-integer powers; it's an infinite series converging for |x| < 1.

slides.title: Full Problem: Expansion and Coefficient Finding
slides.storyContext: Expand (x² + 2/x)⁶ and find the constant term (no x).

example.problem: Use the binomial theorem; the general term is Tᵣ₊₁ = ⁶Cᵣ (x²)⁶⁻ʳ (2/x)ʳ = ⁶Cᵣ × 2ʳ × x¹²⁻³ʳ. For constant term, set 12 − 3r = 0, so r = 4.

slides.inSimpleWords: Write the general term, set the exponent of x to zero, solve for r, then calculate that term's coefficient.

image.alt: Full Problem: Expansion and Coefficient Finding — Binomial Theorem

slides.title: Properties and Identities
slides.storyContext: Priya discovers patterns: 'ⁿC₀ + ⁿC₁ + ... + ⁿCₙ = 2ⁿ. But what if we alternate signs?' Dr. Verma: 'Then we get 0 (for n > 0).'

points.label: Sum of coefficients
points.text: ⁿC₀ + ⁿC₁ + ... + ⁿCₙ = 2ⁿ (set a = b = 1).

points.label: Alternating sum
points.text: ⁿC₀ − ⁿC₁ + ⁿC₂ − ... = 0 (for n > 0) (set a = 1, b = −1).

points.label: Pascal's identity
points.text: ⁿCᵣ + ⁿCᵣ₊₁ = ⁿ⁺¹Cᵣ₊₁.

example.problem: Verify: ⁴C₀ − ⁴C₁ + ⁴C₂ − ⁴C₃ + ⁴C₄ = ?

slides.inSimpleWords: Binomial identities come from setting a and b to specific values in (a + b)ⁿ.

slides.title: Challenge: Irrational Expansion
slides.storyContext: Arjun uses the binomial series to approximate √(1 + x) for small x. The series is (1 + x)^{1/2} = 1 + x/2 − x²/8 + x³/16 − .... Find the first four terms and approximate √1.04.

example.problem: Use the binomial series to approximate √1.04 with 4 terms.

slides.inSimpleWords: The binomial series gives a polynomial approximation for non-integer powers; use the first few terms for a good estimate.

image.alt: Challenge: Irrational Expansion — Binomial Theorem

slides.title: The Binomial Theorem: Key Takeaways

points.text: Binomial theorem: (a + b)ⁿ = Σ ⁿCᵣ aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ (r = 0 to n).
General term: Tᵣ₊₁ = ⁿCᵣ aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ — find individual terms without full expansion.
Pascal's triangle gives binomial coefficients; row n has entries ⁿC₀, ⁿC₁, ..., ⁿCₙ.
Sum of coefficients: ⁿC₀ + ⁿC₁ + ... + ⁿCₙ = 2ⁿ.
Binomial series for non-integer n: (1 + x)ⁿ = Σ ⁿCᵣ xʳ (r = 0 to ∞), valid for |x| < 1.
Use the series to approximate irrational numbers and functions.

slides.inSimpleWords: The binomial theorem expands (a + b)ⁿ efficiently; it applies to integer powers and, as an infinite series, to non-integer powers.

image.alt: The Binomial Theorem: Key Takeaways — Binomial Theorem
